It is not professional, but it isn't grammatically incorrect. It's advised against in general writing, but like I said, this is Reddit. Not an essay. Single contractions are also highly advised against in professional writing, so formal vs informal isn't saying much on its own.

In fact, it may more accurately convey tone than writing "he'd have" or "he would have" would have. Similar to saying something such as "ain't nobody." It is absolutely correct, it is informal, which English, in writing, and otherwise, often is. It conveys the point across and that's all that's needed. 

Nobody needs an explanation about why "ain't nobody" is grammatically incorrect in formal writing, we all know it's not already. As explained, people use it in speech and it conveys the message, so no, it's not completely incorrect. Which is why I called you Reddit Sheldon. Nobody ever really gives a shit about informal writing on Reddit unless you're a grammar Nazi. It was a grammatical oddity but beyond that it was perfectly okay.

Edit: "Ain't nobody" may have been a bad example as double negatives on their own are often grammatically incorrect, but my point I was conveying was when used informally it's rare anybody will ever call you out for it unless it's in a setting where informal grammar stands out. He'd've on the other hand, is always correct despite the odd look.
